summary: This text distinguishes between 'learning,' which is acquired through human effort, and 'wisdom,' which is a gift from God. The author argues that prioritizing learning over wisdom leads to hypocrisy and conflict, referencing the Pharisees as an example. True progress in society and religion can only happen when wisdom is restored to its proper place, bringing love and certainty.

people.name: Pharisees
people.role: A learned Jewish sect from the Old and New Testaments, cited as an example of those who prioritize learning over wisdom, leading to mischief and discord.

people.name: Sadducees
people.role: A scribal Jewish sect, mentioned alongside the Pharisees as examples of the learned who cause trouble and resist the divinely inspired.

people.name: Prophets
people.role: Figures from the Old Testament who were resisted by the learned (Pharisees and Sadducees) and are implicitly associated with Divine Wisdom.

people.name: Apostles
people.role: Figures from the New Testament who, like the Prophets, were resisted by the learned and are implicitly associated with Divine Wisdom.

concepts: The distinction between Learning (Doctrina) as a human-acquired 'natural gift' and Wisdom (Sapientia) as a divine 'gift of God'.
The argument that prioritizing learning over wisdom leads to hypocrisy, discord, and the loss of love and certainty.
The use of the Pharisees and Sadducees as historical examples of learned groups who resisted divinely-inspired figures (Prophets and Apostles).
The hope for a restoration of wisdom to its rightful dominion, which would lead to progress in both the Church and in arts and sciences.
